title: Seva as spirituality
hookLine: service is not a side activity; it is the path

lines: NOT PAID. CONTENT TO BE THERE.
cards: At a gurdwara door, you take off your shoes. Someone behind a counter takes them, slides them onto a rack, and hands you a token. When you come out, they find your pair and hand it back, sometimes wiped clean.
You met that counter on day eight. Who's behind it? Nobody you hired.
A college student, a retired engineer, a shopkeeper on his day off, a grandmother who has done it for years. Not paid, not there to be noticed, handling strangers' shoes, and content to be there.
Today asks why that counter sits close to the center of Sikh spiritual life.

teach.h: SEVA: SERVICE, NO WAGE, NO SCORE.
teach.b: Seva is selfless service: work done for others with no wage and no score kept. In a gurdwara it looks like cooking and serving in the langar, washing dishes, sweeping floors, minding shoes.
Outside, it's anything done for someone who needs it. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak puts it plainly.

teach.h: EARN SERVICE HERE, IN THE WORLD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: earn service here in the world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in the world. Not after.
Not somewhere holier. Here, at the shoe counter, at the stove. Tradition tells a story.
During a battle, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya went across the field with a water skin, giving water to the wounded, including soldiers from the other side. Some Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh.
When the Guru asked him why, tradition says, Ghanaiya answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru's face in everyone. And the Guru gave him ointment as well, so he could dress their wounds too.
Why is seva the path and not a side activity? It works on the very thing we met a few days ago: haumai, ego. It's hard to hold onto I, me, mine while you're scrubbing someone else's pot.
So seva isn't a break from prayer. Sikhs speak of it as a form of prayer: the hands remembering what the lips say. The hope is service without the self in the way: no photo, no thank-you required.

how: Sikhs do seva in gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, and outside them through volunteer service, understood as a spiritual practice rather than a side activity.

o: a set of chores new members must do before joining
a donation paid to a gurdwara to earn a blessing
selfless service, done in the world as the path itself

games.q: service as the path: tap the pairs.
p: serve here, find a seat in the court
water for the wounded on both sides

s: seva means only cooking in the langar kitchen
it also means sweeping, washing, minding shoes, and serving anyone in need.
in the story, Bhai Ghanaiya gave water only to his own side
tradition says he gave water to the wounded from both sides.
Guru Nanak links service in this world with a seat in the divine court
in Sri Raag, in paraphrase: earn service here.

games.q: you're Bhai Ghanaiya on the battlefield with a water skin, and wounded men from the other side are calling for water. what do you do?
o: give water only to your own side.
give water to anyone wounded, from either side.
leave the field; it isn't your fight.
games.why: tradition says he gave water to all, saw the Guru's face in everyone, and the Guru gave him ointment too.

practice: Bring to mind one small act of service nobody would ever thank you for, a dish in the sink, a neighbor's bin, a message to someone who is struggling, and picture doing it slowly, with care, the way someone at the counter hands back a stranger's shoes.
Notice any part of you that wants credit, and let it rest. If you pray, offer the act quietly with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Seva as spirituality. Selfless service, done in the world, not beside the path but as the path itself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: service is the path. The hands remember what the lips say. Rest well.
